spec.title: Dry-run: active-passive failover
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. The mechanics of promoting a replica are easy — the hard part is making sure two nodes never both think they're primary.

steps.title: Health checks decide when to failover, not humans
steps.explain: A monitor pings the primary on a short interval. One missed check is noise — a network blip, a GC pause — so failover triggers only after several consecutive failures, trading a few seconds of detection delay for not failing over on a false alarm.

steps.title: The naive promotion — races with the old primary
steps.explain: Just telling the replica 'you're primary now' is broken if the old primary is actually still alive — maybe it was a network partition on the monitor's side, not a real crash. Both nodes would now accept writes.

steps.title: Fix: fence the old primary before promoting
steps.explain: Fencing means making the old primary provably unable to accept writes before the new one starts — revoke its access token, pull its network route, or have it self-check a lease and step down. Only after fencing succeeds does promotion happen, closing the split-brain window.
steps.saysOutLoud: I promote only after the old primary is fenced, not just presumed dead.

steps.title: A lease makes the primary self-demote if isolated
steps.explain: Instead of relying only on an external fence, the primary itself holds a renewable lease from a coordination service. If it can't renew — because it's the one that's actually partitioned — it stops accepting writes on its own, which is a second independent guard against split brain.

steps.title: Traffic redirection is a routing layer, not the app
steps.explain: Once the new primary is confirmed, clients need to find it — a floating virtual IP (VRRP/keepalived), a DNS record with a short TTL, or a proxy layer that watches the coordinator, are the usual mechanisms. The application code above never changes an IP address itself; it only flips a role.

steps.title: Replaying the write gap after recovery
steps.explain: When the old primary comes back, it's behind and must not simply resume as primary — it rejoins as a replica and catches up from the new primary's log before it's trusted with anything, otherwise it could reintroduce writes that were already superseded.

spec.closing: If they ask about active-active instead: it removes the failover pause entirely but trades it for needing conflict resolution on every write, not just during an outage — worth it only if the write conflict rate is low enough to make that cheap.
